extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or quality management system plus technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), the provider may choose internal control or notified body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied.

Annex VII (notified body) assessment is mandatory for biometric identification systems and certain critical infrastructure AI systems, while most other high-risk AI systems may use the Annex VI self-assessment route.

For high-risk AI systems covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Section A of Annex I (e.g., machinery, medical devices), providers must follow the conformity assessment procedures of that sectoral legislation, with notified bodies also verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements.
Substantial modifications to a high-risk AI system require a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in systems designed to continue learning after deployment.

For the conformity assessment procedure under Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except where the high-risk AI system is intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, or asylum authorities or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body.

Where necessary to assess conformity with Chapter III Section 2 requirements, and after other reasonable means have proven insufficient, a notified body may be granted access to the training and trained models of the AI system, subject to IP and confidentiality protections.

Article 46 allows a market surveillance authority to derogate from the standard conformity assessment procedure and authorise placing a specific high-risk AI system on the market for exceptional reasons (public security, health, environment, key infrastructure) for a limited period.

The notified body assessment under Annex VII involves verifying the provider's quality management system against Article 17 requirements and examining technical documentation for compliance with essential requirements in Chapter III, Section 2.
Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 establishes administrative rules for identification numbers and lists of notified bodies under the AI Act.
The Council is working on a document (ST-7322-2026) assigning 'AIP' codes to categorize AI systems under Annex I for the scope of notified body designations under Article 30.

A Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV listing categories and corresponding AI system types for the Commission's NANDO information system, to integrate AI Act high-risk requirements with existing frameworks like Regulation (EU) 2018/1139.
As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for AI Act conformity assessment is still being built, with designation processes ongoing across member states and limited capacity.
As of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act.

As of October 2025, the NANDO system lists 51 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, but these are designations under the Medical Devices Regulation/IVDR, not the AI Act specifically.

Post-2026, notified bodies designated under the AI Act are expected to begin conducting AI Act-specific conformity assessments, intersecting with existing MDR/IVDR notified body assessments for medical device AI.

A news blog reports that under a final text agreed in September 2026, the deadline for Annex III high-risk AI obligations was moved to 2 August 2029 (from a previously reported 2 December 2027), citing lack of readiness of harmonised standards and notified bodies.

Other sources describe August 2026 as the key deadline by which high-risk AI obligations fully apply, with providers needing to complete conformity assessment, CE marking, and registration by that date.

Providers must issue an EU declaration of conformity referencing the Article 43 procedure followed (Annex VI or Annex VII) and notified body information where applicable, before placing high-risk AI systems/SaaS products on the market.

Article 43(5) empowers the European Commission to adopt delegated acts updating Annex VI and Annex VII conformity assessment procedures in light of technical progress, without need for full legislative revision.

For the Cyber Resilience Act (a separate but related regulation), as of late June 2026 zero notified bodies had been designated in NANDO, with a target of sufficient notified body capacity by 11 December 2026 and full application from 11 December 2027.

report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Requirements and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43—internal control (Annex VI) and notified body assessment involving quality management and technical documentation review (Annex VII)—with the route depending on the AI system category and applicable standards (low-medium confidence). Despite the regulatory framework being in place, evidence in this research suggests that as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, creating significant implementation uncertainty, and sources disagree on the exact compliance deadlines (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or a combined quality management system and technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric systems under point 1 of Annex III, providers may choose between internal control or notified body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some interpretive sources suggest Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on Annex VI self-assessment, though this categorization is only partially corroborated (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation (Annex I, Section A—e.g., machinery, medical devices), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific requirements alongside existing sectoral ones (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Providers may generally choose any notified body under Annex VII, except where systems are intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Notified bodies may, where necessary and after other means prove insufficient, access training data and trained models, subject to IP protections (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard procedures to authorize market placement for exceptional public security, health, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Evidence on actual notified body designations under the AI Act is sparse and low-confidence. As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was reportedly still being built, with designation processes ongoing but limited capacity (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). A separate source claims that as of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, as of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies—but these are designations under medical device regulations, not the AI Act itself (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). For comparison, the related Cyber Resilience Act reportedly had zero designated notified bodies as of late June 2026 (low confidence) ([CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)).

Procedural groundwork is underway: a Council document (ST-7322-2026) is reportedly developing 'AIP' codes to categorize Annex I AI systems for notified body designation scope (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), and a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV integrating AI Act requirements into the NANDO system (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources sharply disagree on deadlines: multiple sources cite August 2, 2026 as the deadline for high-risk obligations (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)), while one unverified news blog claims a September 2026 agreement pushed this to August 2, 2029, citing unreadiness of standards and notified bodies (low confidence, flagged below 0.4) ([ai-act-news-blog](https://ai-act-news-blog.example/annex-iii-deadline-update)). This claim lacks corroboration from any official EU legal text. Several additional low-confidence claims (0.03–0.17) regarding delegated acts, Article 35 administrative rules, and declaration of conformity requirements should be treated cautiously given weak sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No official EU source in this research confirms the current count of AI Act-specific notified body designations as of October 2026. The legal status of the alleged 2029 deadline extension remains unverified against OJ publication or amending regulation. It is unclear whether COM(2025) 836 and ST-7322-2026 have been formally adopted. The relationship between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and AI Act designation—automatic extension versus separate assessment—is unresolved. Precise criteria distinguishing which Annex III categories require Annex VII versus Annex VI assessment remain only partially documented.

# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Requirements and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems under Article 43—internal control (Annex VI) and notified body assessment involving quality management and technical documentation review (Annex VII)—with the route depending on the AI system category and applicable standards (low-medium confidence). Despite the regulatory framework being in place, evidence in this research suggests that as of early-to-mid 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated specifically under the AI Act, creating significant implementation uncertainty, and sources disagree on the exact compliance deadlines (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Article 43 of the AI Act establishes two primary conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems: internal control under Annex VI, or a combined quality management system and technical documentation assessment by a notified body under Annex VII (low confidence) ([VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai), [FPF](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)). For biometric systems under point 1 of Annex III, providers may choose between internal control or notified body assessment depending on whether harmonised standards or common specifications have been applied (low confidence) ([Futurium](https://futurium.ec.europa.eu/sites/default/files/2021-10/Kop_EU%20Artificial%20Intelligence%20Act%20-%20The%20European%20Approach%20to%20AI_21092021_0.pdf)). Some interpretive sources suggest Annex VII assessment is mandatory for biometric identification and certain critical infrastructure systems, while most other high-risk systems may rely on Annex VI self-assessment, though this categorization is only partially corroborated (low confidence) ([Quantamix](https://quantamixsolutions.com/insights/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation (Annex I, Section A—e.g., machinery, medical devices), providers must follow the sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific requirements alongside existing sectoral ones (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), [VDE](https://www.vde.com/topics-en/artificial-intelligence/blog/conformity-assessment-high-risk-ai)). Substantial modifications trigger a new conformity assessment, except for predetermined changes in continuously-learning systems (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Providers may generally choose any notified body under Annex VII, except where systems are intended for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, or EU institutional use, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority acts as the notified body (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/ga/ai-act/article-43)). Notified bodies may, where necessary and after other means prove insufficient, access training data and trained models, subject to IP protections (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk - Annex VII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-7)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to derogate from standard procedures to authorize market placement for exceptional public security, health, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Evidence on actual notified body designations under the AI Act is sparse and low-confidence. As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem was reportedly still being built, with designation processes ongoing but limited capacity (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act)). A separate source claims that as of April 2026, no notified bodies had been formally designated under the AI Act (low confidence) ([aiact-navigator](https://aiact-navigator.com/blog/eu-ai-act-medical-devices-mdr-ivdr-interplay-guide)). By contrast, as of October 2025, NANDO listed 51 MDR-designated and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies—but these are designations under medical device regulations, not the AI Act itself (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051)). For comparison, the related Cyber Resilience Act reportedly had zero designated notified bodies as of late June 2026 (low confidence) ([CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)).

Procedural groundwork is underway: a Council document (ST-7322-2026) is reportedly developing 'AIP' codes to categorize Annex I AI systems for notified body designation scope (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), and a Commission proposal (COM(2025) 836) would create a new Annex XIV integrating AI Act requirements into the NANDO system (medium confidence) ([Council of the EU](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources sharply disagree on deadlines: multiple sources cite August 2, 2026 as the deadline for high-risk obligations (low confidence) ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [sota.io](https://sota.io/blog/eu-ai-act-eu-declaration-conformity-ce-marking-registration-saas-providers-2026)), while one unverified news blog claims a September 2026 agreement pushed this to August 2, 2029, citing unreadiness of standards and notified bodies (low confidence, flagged below 0.4) ([ai-act-news-blog](https://ai-act-news-blog.example/annex-iii-deadline-update)). This claim lacks corroboration from any official EU legal text. Several additional low-confidence claims (0.03–0.17) regarding delegated acts, Article 35 administrative rules, and declaration of conformity requirements should be treated cautiously given weak sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No official EU source in this research confirms the current count of AI Act-specific notified body designations as of October 2026. The legal status of the alleged 2029 deadline extension remains unverified against OJ publication or amending regulation. It is unclear whether COM(2025) 836 and ST-7322-2026 have been formally adopted. The relationship between existing MDR/IVDR notified bodies and AI Act designation—automatic extension versus separate assessment—is unresolved. Precise criteria distinguishing which Annex III categories require Annex VII versus Annex VI assessment remain only partially documented.
